claims.claim: Hewitt argues that a Curse of Strahd room's gothic atmosphere is established by the physical objects in its description rather than by naming the mood.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 15 Dec 2024
claims.quote: gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue

claims.claim: Hewitt finds Strahd's suggested descriptions unchanged between texts even where his alignment changed.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 15 Dec 2024
claims.quote: descriptions do not change from one text to the other

claims.claim: Hines contrasts Gygax's counterintuitive trap style with fifth edition's preference for clarity in description.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 19 Mar 2023
claims.quote: style of heroism and clarity in description
claims.page: section on Tomb of Horrors and OSR mechanics

claims.claim: Peterson reports that economics dominate the events reported in Arneson's 1971 in-world campaign newsletter.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: Economics play a large role in the events described

claims.claim: The items Peterson lists from that newsletter are civic and financial: a tax collection, restitution paid for damage done by a wizard's dragon's offspring, and a ruined tavern.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: pays restitution for damages caused by his dragon

claims.claim: Peterson says the earliest Blackmoor campaign newsletter tells little about the game system but much about the setting and the state of the campaign.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: significant insight into the setting and the state of the campaign

claims.claim: Peterson dates the earliest explicit use of 'immersion' he has found to Pieter Roos in The Wild Hunt #15 (1977).
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 31 Jan 2021
claims.quote: The earliest explicit use I've found was that of Pieter Roos

claims.claim: Peterson identifies Mike Carr's B1 tips as connecting playing your character's role with a call to immerse yourself in the game setting.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 31 Jan 2021, on Mike Carr's B1 (1979)
claims.quote: immerse yourself in the game setting

claims.claim: Alexander's verdict on the form is that location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 19 May 2014

claims.claim: Alexander describes the 1974 sample map's key as instructional rather than practical.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Alexander says Gygax's undivided 'wall of text' key remained the TSR staple for the better part of a decade.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: a staple at TSR for the better part of a decade
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Bob Blake's 1976 Judges Guild keys split each entry with a 'DM Only' section, which Alexander reads as structurally the same move as later boxed text.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Alexander reports that in the original Lost Tamoachan the read-aloud passages were set in quotation marks, and only the 1980 reissue put them in a box.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014

claims.claim: Alexander defines the function of boxed text as marking what a character entering the area learns immediately.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: should be immediately shared with any PC entering the area

claims.claim: The third edition standard format introduced by The Sunless Citadel fixed a set of bold-faced sections that had to appear in one order.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: they appeared in that order and no other
